notes.heading: Overview
points: Solid waste refers to unwanted solid or semi-solid materials generated by human activities
Rapid urbanization and industrialization have increased solid waste generation
Improper waste management leads to severe environmental and health problems
Solid waste management is a key part of sustainable urban governance

notes.heading: Solid Waste Management – Definition
points: Solid waste management is the systematic handling of waste from generation to disposal
Includes collection, segregation, transportation, treatment, and final disposal
Aims to minimize environmental impact and maximize resource recovery
Focuses on reducing, reusing, and recycling waste (3R principle)
Essential for maintaining public health and urban cleanliness

notes.heading: Sources of Solid Waste – Overview
points: Solid waste is generated from multiple human activities
Major sources include residential, commercial, industrial, and institutional sectors
Agricultural and construction activities also contribute significantly
Composition varies depending on lifestyle and economic development
Urban areas generate higher and more complex waste

notes.heading: Residential Sources
points: Household kitchen waste (food scraps, vegetable waste)
Paper, plastics, glass, and metal waste
Sanitary waste (diapers, sanitary products)
Old furniture and household items
Electronic waste from homes

notes.heading: Commercial Sources
points: Waste from shops, markets, and offices
Packaging materials like plastic and cardboard
Food waste from restaurants and hotels
Discarded goods and inventory waste
High volume in urban commercial centers

notes.heading: Industrial Sources
points: Manufacturing waste from factories
Chemical waste and hazardous residues
Metal scraps, slag, and fly ash
Packaging and industrial by-products
Often requires special disposal methods

notes.heading: Institutional Sources
points: Waste from schools, hospitals, and government offices
Biomedical waste from healthcare facilities
Paper waste and office supplies
Laboratory chemical waste
Requires segregation and safe handling

notes.heading: Agricultural Sources
points: Crop residues and stubble
Animal manure and farm waste
Agrochemical containers and packaging
Dead plant material
Often reused or burned, causing pollution

notes.heading: Construction and Demolition Waste
points: Concrete, bricks, and rubble
Wood and metal scraps
Soil and excavation debris
Glass and tiles
Major contributor in urban expansion

notes.heading: Electronic Waste (E-Waste)
points: Discarded electronic devices like computers and phones
Contains hazardous metals like lead and mercury
Rapidly increasing due to digitalization
Requires specialized recycling systems
Major environmental concern in cities

notes.heading: Effects of Solid Waste – Overview
points: Solid waste mismanagement affects environment, health, and economy
Leads to pollution of air, water, and soil
Creates breeding grounds for disease vectors
Causes visual and aesthetic pollution
Affects overall quality of urban life

notes.heading: Environmental Effects
points: Soil contamination due to leachate from landfills
Water pollution from waste runoff
Air pollution from burning waste
Methane emission from decomposition in landfills
Loss of biodiversity in affected areas

notes.heading: Health Effects
points: Spread of diseases like cholera and typhoid
Respiratory problems due to burning waste
Skin infections and allergies
Exposure to toxic chemicals and heavy metals
Increased risk of vector-borne diseases (mosquitoes, flies)

notes.heading: Economic Effects
points: High cost of waste management systems
Loss of recyclable materials
Reduced tourism in polluted areas
Healthcare burden due to pollution-related diseases
Decreased land value in waste-affected regions

notes.heading: Social Effects
points: Poor living conditions in urban slums
Inequality in waste disposal services
Public nuisance and foul odors
Conflict over landfill sites
Reduced quality of life in urban areas

notes.heading: Methane Emissions from Waste
points: Organic waste decomposition in landfills produces methane
Methane is a potent greenhouse gas
Contributes to global warming
Can be captured for energy production
Important in climate change discussions

notes.heading: Leachate Formation
points: Liquid formed when rainwater percolates through waste
Contains toxic chemicals and heavy metals
Pollutes groundwater and surface water
Difficult to treat if not managed properly
Major environmental hazard from landfills

name: Control Measures of Solid Waste, Solid Waste Management Rules & Hazardous Waste Management

notes.heading: Overview
points: Solid waste control focuses on reducing, treating, and safely disposing waste to minimize environmental damage
India has legal frameworks like Solid Waste Management Rules and Hazardous Waste Management Rules
Hazardous waste requires special handling due to its toxic and dangerous nature
These systems aim to protect environment, health, and promote resource recovery

notes.heading: Control Measures of Solid Waste – Overview
points: Control measures aim to reduce waste generation and improve management efficiency
Based on hierarchy: Reduce → Reuse → Recycle → Recover → Dispose
Focus on segregation at source and scientific disposal
Involves government, industries, and public participation
Key part of sustainable urban development

notes.heading: Waste Segregation at Source
points: Separation of waste at household or generation point
Wet waste (organic) and dry waste (plastic, paper, metal)
Hazardous waste separated separately
Reduces burden on treatment systems
Improves recycling efficiency

notes.heading: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle (3R Principle)
points: Reduce: Minimize waste generation at source
Reuse: Use materials multiple times before disposal
Recycle: Process waste into reusable materials
Recover: Extract energy from waste (waste-to-energy)
Disposal: Final safe disposal in landfills

notes.heading: Waste Treatment Methods
points: Composting for organic waste
Incineration for hazardous and non-recyclable waste
Anaerobic digestion producing biogas
Recycling of plastics, metals, and paper
Sanitary landfills for final disposal

notes.heading: Public Participation
points: Awareness campaigns on waste segregation
Community-level waste management programs
Swachh Bharat Mission initiatives
Involvement of NGOs and local bodies
Behavioral change towards waste reduction

notes.heading: Solid Waste Management Rules – Overview
points: Issued under Environment Protection Act, 1986
Revised rules: Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016
Applies to urban and rural areas
Focus on segregation, processing, and scientific disposal
Replaced earlier Municipal Solid Waste Rules (2000)

notes.heading: Key Features of SWM Rules 2016
points: Mandatory segregation of waste at source
User fees for waste generation and collection
Waste processing and composting encouraged
Ban on open burning of waste
Integration of informal waste pickers

notes.heading: Role of Local Authorities
points: Collection and transportation of waste
Setting up waste processing facilities
Ensuring compliance of rules
Public awareness generation
Monitoring and enforcement

notes.heading: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
points: Producers are responsible for end-of-life disposal of products
Applicable mainly to plastic and e-waste
Encourages eco-friendly product design
Promotes recycling and reuse systems
Shifts burden from municipalities to producers

notes.heading: Plastic Waste Management Rules
points: Focus on reducing plastic pollution
Ban on single-use plastics in many regions
EPR for plastic producers
Segregation and recycling mandatory
Encourages alternatives to plastic

notes.heading: Hazardous Waste Management (HWM) – Overview
points: Hazardous waste contains substances that are toxic, reactive, or flammable
Can cause serious harm to human health and environment
Requires strict handling, transport, and disposal norms
Governed by Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016
Aligned with international conventions like Basel Convention

notes.heading: Types of Hazardous Waste
points: Chemical waste from industries
Biomedical waste from hospitals
E-waste containing heavy metals
Radioactive waste from nuclear sources
Pesticide and pesticide container waste

notes.heading: Sources of Hazardous Waste
points: Chemical industries and refineries
Pharmaceutical industries
Healthcare facilities
Mining and metallurgical processes
Laboratories and research institutions

notes.heading: Hazardous Waste Management Rules (2016)
points: Classification and identification of hazardous waste
Authorization required for handling and disposal
Manifest system for tracking waste movement
Safe storage and transportation norms
Environmentally sound disposal methods

notes.heading: Treatment and Disposal Methods
points: Incineration for toxic waste
Secure landfilling in designated sites
Chemical treatment to neutralize hazards
Recycling of recoverable materials
Export of waste under Basel Convention rules

notes.heading: Basel Convention
points: International treaty to control transboundary movement of hazardous waste
Aims to reduce hazardous waste generation
Ensures environmentally sound management
Prevents dumping of waste in developing countries
India is a signatory

notes.heading: Effects of Improper Hazardous Waste Management
points: Severe soil and water contamination
Air pollution from toxic emissions
Cancer and neurological disorders in humans
Bioaccumulation in food chain
Long-term ecological damage
